toc.title: A quick review of the autonomic nervous system
Shutdown is supposed to be brief
A challenge: can you validate yourself?

blocks.p: At first, my clients and my students predictably invalidate their emotions without even realizing it. And we all do this on some level. It's hard to notice and allow our emotions compassionately. We want our difficult emotions to go away. So we ignore them, we stuff them down, we judge ourselves, and many, many other means of invalidation.

Of course, I get it. Our emotions are potentially very difficult, especially from shutdown: empty, lonely, sad, hopeless, maybe even weak, just to name a few. But the reality is, to get through these emotions and toward safety, you need to actually allow them compassionately. And the first step in that process is validation.
Let's look at what shutdown and stillness are, how they connect, and then how validation starts the process of self-regulation. There's a little challenge at the end about validating yourself.

blocks.h: A quick review of the autonomic nervous system

blocks.p: Ever so basically and briefly: the body can be in a state of safety. From safety, it shifts to flight. From flight to fight. From fight to shutdown or freeze.

By now you might know about the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). It's a great metaphor from Deb Dana that illustrates that the autonomic nervous system and these different states act like a ladder. We go down in a certain sequence, and we can't really skip. And we come back up the ladder in the reverse sequence. So we go down from safety, to flight, to fight, to shutdown or freeze. To come out of that, we go from shutdown or freeze, to fight, to flight, and then to safety.

Shutdown can be activated as a response to an acute emergency, a life threat. It's activated when you can't escape and can't be aggressive, or when running away or being aggressive hasn't worked against some sort of danger. Then the body goes into shutdown. It collapses in the face of life threat. This first path to trauma is probably more associated with freeze, but shutdown is a possibility as well.

The second path to trauma is the chronic disruption of connectedness. This is where the impulses to connect with a safe other are repeatedly unmet or rejected, which results in a chronic defensive state. That could be any defensive state. But based on my client work, there's commonly some shutdown incorporated in this. If you can't connect with a safe other, or you're repeatedly rejected by one, some shutdown seems to be present. By the time people get to therapy and coaching, there might be more of it, but it's usually there.

blocks.h: Shutdown is supposed to be brief

blocks.p: Shutdown is not supposed to be ongoing. Even in the wild, a mammal is supposed to enter shutdown as a last resort in the face of a life threat, and it's quick. The mammal goes into it and comes right back out once it neurocepts that it has the potential to do so. Then it enters its fight activation, then flight, and then it gets to safety and accesses its safety state. That's it. That's how it's supposed to be.
But as humans, we get stuck in shutdown, which I'm sure you know. And stuck shutdown brings pretty distinct experiences, especially compared to fight, flight, and safety:

ul: Socially: we're more withdrawn. We disconnect from others. Disconnection is kind of a theme with shutdown.
Emotionally: we're more disconnected, with more depression and feelings of emptiness, and a lot more.
Cognitively: we have thoughts that things are hopeless, that we're worthless, that we're helpless.

blocks.p: Those are the general stuck shutdown experiences. Maybe you can relate.
Stillness is the combination of the shutdown state plus the safety state. It's the ability to immobilize without fear.

Right now, on some level, we're all immobile. So we have enough safety in our system to be immobile and be okay with it, hopefully without any fear. Stillness is very important. Intimacy with another person, self-reflection, using the restroom, sitting in class, getting desk work done: all of these involve immobilizing and being okay with it.

Us mammals have this safety state, these ventral vagal pathways, that can repurpose or combine with the defensive states and turn them into something else: a mixed state. Safety is great for optimizing resources by itself, and when it's combined with the defensive states, it helps optimize resources too, especially for prosocial functions.

Safety plus shutdown alone is stillness. Stillness with another is intimacy. And intimacy doesn't necessarily mean physical. It means connection: we're immobile, we're in stillness, but able to connect and co-regulate with another. So safety repurposes shutdown. It turns a dominant shutdown state into stillness, or into intimacy with another.

All of you have some safety. All of you have some shutdown. We just want that balance to look different. As we have more safety, we can access more stillness. We can be in the present moment and be okay with it. We can immobilize and be okay with it.

Building more safety, and with it more stillness and more inner peace, happens through top-down cognitions, environmental and sensory safety cues, and safety anchoring with mindfulness of those cues. But the first step is validating shutdown.
Validation is acknowledging what's true, what's happening internally. We're focused more on emotions and cognitions here, but it's simply acknowledging what is true. It can sound like:
All of these are validating. It's simply acknowledging what you feel or what you're thinking.

Validation is not being okay with, or liking, what is true. You can validate that you feel miserable and not like it. I'm not saying you have to like it or be okay with it. You can say "I feel sad" and not be okay with that at all. You're just acknowledging: I do feel sad, even though I don't like it.

Validation is also not accepting that your experience is permanent. I don't believe shutdown is permanent. I don't believe feeling empty or heavy is permanent. Personally, I think these are temporary things.
Invalidation is judging yourself. It sounds like "There's something wrong with me" or "Other people aren't like this." Maybe you can relate to those words.

Invalidation is minimizing, denying, or using other cognitive skills to lessen the true nature of your experience. It can sound like "It's not a big deal" or "I just need to keep my mind off of it." I hear that a lot from my clients.
Invalidation is labeling or diagnosing your experience. This could sound like "I feel distracted because of my ADHD," or "Maybe I have CPTSD."

I had a client who was going through a divorce. She had grief, regrets, sadness, a little bit of anger. All kinds of emotions that I think are pretty normal for a major life change. Validating for her would be acknowledging how she feels. She went to a couples therapist with her then-husband, and the couples therapist saw her crying and emoting and said, "Seems like something's off about you. I wonder if you have CPTSD."

To me, that is invalidating. That's diagnosing. That's labeling. Diagnoses and labels have their role, and this isn't a discussion about that. But I think they can be misused, especially if you're searching for "What's wrong with me? What's my diagnosis? What's my label?" At that point, I think it becomes invalidation.
You might be saying, "I don't want to validate this. I don't like it. I don't want to feel it. I don't want to pay attention to it at all."
Well, how can you exit shutdown if you don't acknowledge that it exists? If you don't acknowledge the experiences of shutdown, how can you take that next step? To me, validating it is the first step.

What would the alternative be? Ignoring it, minimizing it, repressing it, stuffing it down. Likely you've done some of these things, or are doing them now. How has that worked out for you? Maybe it's gotten you to where you are now, and that's a good thing. Maybe it got you through it. But maybe it's done as much as it can, and it's not really going to help you anymore. It's okay to say, "These played a role and helped me deal with things, but they've outlived their usefulness, and I'm ready for something different now."

You validate by acknowledging what is true, as best you can. That means acknowledging, or naming, what you feel as you feel it. You have to be honest with yourself. If you're judging yourself, that isn't validating.
Your feelings are there. I don't think you're making any of this up. I don't think it's random. Your state is likely shutdown, or some shutdown within you, and you have to be honest about that.

All of this happens in the present moment. If you're trying to keep your mind off it, or stuffing it down, you exist in the present moment, but experientially you're not in it. Being honest with yourself comes after you ground yourself in the present moment enough to be able to be honest. So:

ol: Take a deep breath, and let it out slowly.
As you exhale, say, "Yeah, I feel..." and name what's there.

blocks.p: The good news is you've already validated yourself on some level. You're here. Something is uncomfortable enough, and you were honest with yourself enough, that you showed up. We just want to take validation a step further.

blocks.h: A challenge: can you validate yourself?

blocks.p: Reflect on these questions. You can write them down if you like, or just think them through.

Could you validate somebody else's emotions? Could you acknowledge them and name them? If I told you, "I feel heavy. I just don't want to do anything," would you be able to say, "Sounds like you feel unmotivated. Sounds like you might feel kind of sad, or numb"? I assume you'd be able to.

If you talked to a therapist or some other helper about your emotions, would they be able to acknowledge what you feel? If you told them, "I think this way, and I feel this way, and I behave this way," would they say, "Yeah, it sounds like you're in a really depressed place"? Hopefully the answer is yes. Hopefully someone else would be able to do that for you.
So can you validate yourself? Can you give that to yourself? That's the point here.
A few more prompts to get your mind going:

ul: How do you feel about validating your experiences?
What emotions and cognitions come up for you when I ask you to validate yourself?
Was validation a normal part of your upbringing?
Would you like to validate yourself more?
